candidates.title: rollup CLI --utf8-payload: an input whose payload is not valid UTF-8 makes `rollup accept/finish/reject` fail after it has already consumed that input, so the application never sees it
candidates.location: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp: finish_request_and_get_next() -> cmt_rollup_finish() (yield rx-accepted, the next input is delivered) -> write_advance_state() -> encode_payload() returns the raw bytes for encoding::utf8 -> nlohmann::json::dump(2) with the default error_handler_t::strict throws type_error.316; the catch in finish_request_and_get_next prints the message and returns 1. The same applies to write_inspect_state and to `rollup gio` responses.
candidates.description: In --utf8-payload mode the CLI writes the payload bytes into a JSON string without checking them. nlohmann::json::dump rejects invalid UTF-8 by throwing. By then cmt_rollup_finish has already accepted (or rejected) the previous request and the machine has delivered the next input, so the tool exits 1, prints nothing on stdout, and the input it took from the rx buffer is lost to the application. The help text and the manual (doc/README.md, 'The rollup command-line utility') promise that "<data> contains arbitrary data in the selected payload encoding", and the manual's own calculator (calc.sh) and docs examples run the loop with `rollup --utf8-payload accept`. Nothing documents that some byte strings cannot be delivered, and the application has no way to find out what the input was. Its only options are to accept the input without processing it (outputs it should emit are missing), to reject an input it would have accepted, or to stop, which leaves the machine halted, never yielding again.
candidates.trigger: Any input sender (untrusted, 'any bytes, any count', THREAT_MODEL section 4) calls InputBox.addInput with a payload that is not valid UTF-8 (for example 0xff, or any binary payload such as a portal-style deposit) to an application whose loop is the documented `rollup --utf8-payload accept|finish` pattern.
candidates.reachability: Reachable from any valid template that runs a --utf8-payload loop: the input record carries arbitrary payload bytes (InputBox only bounds the length), libcmt decodes them correctly, and the throw happens on every such input. Reproduced on the host with the libcmt mock (same rollup.cpp code path).
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? No. The exclusion for applications that are not correctly designed applies only "other than through a defect in guest software that section 3 puts in scope". The trigger is a byte string any sender can submit, and the failing component is the guest tool, not the application.

2 Role: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 is Guest software (AUDIT.md table). THREAT_MODEL.md section 3, Guest software: "A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low."
3 High/Medium cases: none apply. They concern verifiers, the emulator and support components.

4 Critical (strict reading): the application uses the tool as documented ("arbitrary data in the selected payload encoding"; the manual's calculator uses --utf8-payload). It would be correctly designed if the tool worked as documented, and one input makes it deviate from the rollup interface. Either the input is accepted without its outputs (wrong or missing outputs, so the tx-buffer outputs Merkle root is not the one the application defines), or a valid input is rejected, or the application never yields again. Per the section 2 definition, a correctly designed application must, "After each input, ... yield manually with the accepted or the rejected reason" and leave "the outputs Merkle root of every output it accepted". This is an R7 deviation in "The rx buffer, the tx buffer, and the yield interface (contents, lengths, and reason encoding)".

5 Low (alternative reading): if triage holds that UTF-8 mode implies the application only expects UTF-8 payloads, and that a correct application must treat a non-zero exit of `rollup accept` as 'reject the current input', then the tool fails loudly and the defect is Low. The deciding fact is whether the help text's "arbitrary data in the selected payload encoding" promises lossless delivery of every payload in UTF-8 mode. Note that the manual's calc.sh happens to fall back to `rollup reject` on this failure.
candidates.claimed_severity: Critical (strict reading of the section 3 guest-software clause); Low if the documented UTF-8 mode is read as excluding non-UTF-8 inputs
candidates.threat_to_goal: Every input sender can make a documented --utf8-payload application drop or mis-handle an input, or halt for good. The settled state then commits to an outputs Merkle root that leaves out outputs the application's design requires, or to a halted application. The goal promises that a correctly designed application settles the state the transition function defines for its intended behavior. The emulator and the honest operator are unaffected; only the application's own result is.
candidates.evidence: Built libcmt mock and rollup.cpp on the host (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-machine-emulator/549e7dd9-06ba-5ccf-8b17-f8cce9526655/scratchpad/blind10/PERAPPDEV/rollup-mock). Encoded EvmAdvance with payload ff00fe41 (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-machine-emulator/549e7dd9-06ba-5ccf-8b17-f8cce9526655/scratchpad/blind10/PERAPPDEV/bad.bin) and with payload 'hello' (ok.bin). CMT_INPUTS=0:ok.bin rollup --utf8-payload accept -> JSON, rc=0. CMT_INPUTS=0:bad.bin rollup --utf8-payload accept -> stderr '[json.exception.type_error.316] invalid UTF-8 byte at index 0: 0xFF', nothing on stdout, rc=1 (the mock had already loaded the input, as the real driver does). The same input with --base64-payload -> JSON, rc=0.
candidates.test_idea: In a machine built from the guest-tools rootfs (work/images/rootfs.ext2), use entrypoint `rollup --utf8-payload accept > /tmp/req && jq -Rs '{payload:.}' < /tmp/req | rollup --utf8-payload notice && rollup accept || rollup reject`, or any loop that echoes the request as a notice. Deliver an advance whose payload is 0xff. Assert the documented behavior: the machine reaches an rx-accepted yield, and the tx buffer holds the outputs root of exactly one notice containing the request (the input was delivered and representable). Today the first command exits 1 and the machine reaches rx-rejected instead. A host-side variant runs the mock CLI with CMT_INPUTS and asserts rc==0 and that the JSON on stdout carries the payload.

candidates.title: rollup CLI ignores outputs-Merkle-tree persistence errors (/tmp/merkle.dat): after a failed or interrupted save, an emitted output is left out of the outputs Merkle root and the CLI still reports success
candidates.component: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1, sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp class rollup; libcmt src/merkle.c cmt_merkle_load/cmt_merkle_save, src/util.c cmt_util_read_whole_file
candidates.location: rollup.cpp: rollup::rollup() calls cmt_rollup_load_merkle(&m_rollup, "/tmp/merkle.dat") and ignores the result; rollup::~rollup() calls cmt_rollup_save_merkle(...) and ignores the result. write_voucher/write_notice/write_delegate_call_voucher yield the output (cmt_rollup_emit_*), print {"index":n} and return 0 before the destructor tries to save. merkle.c cmt_merkle_load: cmt_util_read_whole_file freads straight into the live cmt_merkle_t and only then checks the length, so a short file leaves a mixed tree. util.c cmt_util_write_whole_file truncates the file (fopen "wb") before writing.
candidates.description: Each `rollup` CLI process keeps the outputs Merkle tree only in /tmp/merkle.dat. It saves the tree after the output has already been yielded to the host, and ignores any save error. If the save fails (ENOSPC or ENOMEM on the /tmp tmpfs, a permission or ownership problem, the process being killed between the yield and the destructor, or a truncated file left by such a kill), the output stays emitted but missing from the tree. The command still exits 0 and prints its index. The next `rollup notice` reuses the same index, and the next `rollup accept` writes to the tx buffer an outputs Merkle root that leaves out an output the host saw. A load error is ignored too: a missing or short file silently restarts from the empty tree, or from a partially overwritten one, which drops every earlier output from the root. The application cannot detect any of this through the documented interface.
candidates.trigger: Needs the save or the load of /tmp/merkle.dat to fail inside the guest. An application that keeps input-derived data on the /tmp tmpfs (the manual's calc.sh already keeps its request file there), or that runs under memory pressure driven by inputs, lets an input sender push the guest toward ENOSPC/ENOMEM or an OOM kill of the `rollup` process after its yield. Directly reproducible with an unwritable /tmp/merkle.dat.
candidates.reachability: The silent-ignore code path runs on every CLI output command. Whether an input alone can make the save fail for a correctly designed application is not demonstrated. It depends on application memory and storage use, which section 2 does not bound. Truncate-then-write usually reuses the freed tmpfs page, which makes plain ENOSPC unlikely.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? Possibly. If the only triggers are application misuse or guest-internal resource exhaustion that a correctly designed application must avoid, the trigger is outside the model. It is not a host fault: /tmp is guest state.

2 Role: machine-guest-tools rollup CLI is Guest software. THREAT_MODEL.md section 3, Guest software: "A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low."
3 High/Medium cases: none apply to guest software.

4 Critical if an input can make the save fail for an application that uses the CLI as documented. The tx buffer then holds a wrong outputs Merkle root (the section 2 definition requires "the outputs Merkle root of every output it accepted"). That is an R7 deviation in the tx buffer, and outputs the host saw become unprovable under A5.
5 Low otherwise: a real defect, in that errors are swallowed and success is reported, which violates no rule unless the trigger is reachable.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (Critical if triage finds an input-driven save failure for a documented application)
candidates.threat_to_goal: A silently wrong outputs Merkle root in the settled state makes a correctly emitted output unprovable, and makes later outputs reuse indices. The guest tool hides the condition, so the application cannot reject the input to recover.
candidates.evidence: In a private mount namespace with a tmpfs /tmp (host /tmp untouched), with the host-built rollup CLI against the libcmt mock: two `rollup notice` calls normally return index 0 and 1. With /tmp/merkle.dat made unwritable (a directory), both return {"index":0} with rc=0, so the second output is pushed onto an empty tree and the first is lost from the root.
candidates.test_idea: Inside a machine with the guest-tools rootfs, use the entrypoint `rollup accept; mkdir -p /tmp/merkle.dat 2>/dev/null; echo '{"payload":"0x01"}' | rollup notice; echo '{"payload":"0x02"}' | rollup notice; rollup accept`, or make the file read-only after the first save. Deliver one advance, and assert either that a `rollup notice` exits non-zero when its tree is not persisted, or that the tx-buffer root at the rx-accepted yield equals the root of both notices (compute it with cartesi.hash-tree frontier). Today both notices report index 0 and the root covers one leaf.

candidates.title: rollup-http-server delivers block_timestamp in seconds, but its documented API (openapi rollup.yaml, linked from the server README) defines it as milliseconds
candidates.component: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1, rollup-http/rollup-http-server src/rollup/mod.rs AdvanceMetadata::from; documented API cartesi openapi rollup.yaml (Metadata.block_timestamp)
candidates.location: rollup-http-server/src/rollup/mod.rs: impl From<cmt_rollup_advance_t> for AdvanceMetadata copies block_timestamp: other.block_timestamp, which is the EvmAdvance blockTimestamp = block.timestamp in seconds (doc/README.md: "The block timestamp field is in seconds since the Unix epoch"). rollup.yaml Metadata.block_timestamp: "Unix timestamp of block in milliseconds.", example 1588598533000. That text dates from 2022 (openapi-interfaces commit 4ff0c6e) and the README links to the rollup.yaml of cartesi/rollups.
candidates.description: An application written against the documented HTTP API reads metadata.block_timestamp as milliseconds, but the server passes the raw EvmAdvance value, which is seconds. Any time-dependent logic (deadlines, auctions, vesting, rate limits) is off by a factor of 1000: the application sees dates in January 1970 and treats every deadline expressed in real milliseconds as not yet reached, or reached far too early. The input field is mis-decoded relative to the documented interface on every advance input.
candidates.trigger: Every advance input, whatever its sender, to an HTTP-API application that uses block_timestamp as documented. An input sender can pick inputs whose acceptance depends on the time check, such as bids after a deadline or early withdrawals.
candidates.reachability: Every input from every valid template running rollup-http-server. Deterministic, not data-dependent.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? No exclusion matches. The application follows the documented API; the mismatch is between the guest tool and its own documented interface.

2 Role: machine-guest-tools rollup-http-server is Guest software. THREAT_MODEL.md section 3, Guest software: "A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low."

3 High/Medium cases: none for guest software. "A contradiction between the manual and the behavior on a security-relevant point is a defect in one of the two" applies by analogy to the guest tool's own API document.

4 Critical if triage reads a field delivered under a different unit than documented as an R7 deviation in rx-buffer contents ("mis-decoded input field"): an input then makes a documented application accept or reject or emit outputs other than it would with the documented value.

5 Low under the narrower reading that the yield, accept and reject protocol and the outputs root stay intact and only the application's own logic is affected, so it is a documentation defect. The deciding fact is whether the guest-software clause covers the meaning of decoded input fields or only their bytes.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (Critical under the 'mis-decoded input field is an rx-buffer deviation' reading)
candidates.threat_to_goal: Settled states of HTTP-API applications that rely on time encode decisions taken on a timestamp 1000x off from the documented meaning. The goal holds for the emulator, but the application settles results that differ from its documented design.
candidates.evidence: Code reading of mod.rs, plus the rollup.yaml text retrieved by `git clone` of cartesi/openapi-interfaces (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-machine-emulator/549e7dd9-06ba-5ccf-8b17-f8cce9526655/scratchpad/blind10/PERAPPDEV/oapi/rollup.yaml lines ~380-385). The manual (doc/README.md ~line 4960) states seconds.
candidates.test_idea: Run rollup-http-server in a machine with a tiny HTTP client application that emits metadata.block_timestamp as a notice. Deliver an advance with blockTimestamp=1700000000 and assert that the notice reports 1700000000000 (documented unit), or fix the documentation and assert seconds. Today it reports 1700000000.

candidates.title: rollup CLI `voucher` accepts a `value` shorter than 32 bytes and leaves the rest of the uint256 uninitialized, emitting a voucher with a garbage value
candidates.location: rollup.cpp decode_hex32() only rejects strings longer than 2+64 characters; write_voucher() declares `cmt_abi_u256_t value;` uninitialized and does memcpy(value.data, value_bytes.data(), value_bytes.size()), copying the short big-endian prefix into the most significant bytes.
candidates.description: "0x01" becomes 0x01 followed by 31 bytes of stack garbage, and "0x" is all garbage, instead of being rejected or zero-extended. The voucher (an output, hashed into the outputs Merkle root) carries an unintended, huge ETH value. In the machine the garbage is deterministic, but it is not what the application asked for, and the CLI reports success with an index. The help text says <hex-uint256> is "a big-endian 32-byte unsigned integer in hex", so a short value is outside the documented use. The rollup-http-server instead right-aligns short values correctly.
candidates.trigger: An application that builds `value` as a minimal hex string, for example from an input amount, or passes "0x0"/"0x00". Not an input by itself.
candidates.reachability: Only when the application passes a non-32-byte value, which is not the documented format.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The trigger needs the application to depart from the documented 32-byte format. That is "an application outside its intended use", unless triage reads the missing validation as the defect.

2 Role: Guest software. THREAT_MODEL.md section 3, Guest software: "A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low."
3 High/Medium: none.
4 Critical only if a documented application can reach it; it cannot under the strict 32-byte reading.

5 Low: a real defect (use of uninitialized memory, silent acceptance of malformed input, wrong output) that only an application outside its intended use reaches. Section 8 Low lists "a defect in guest software that only an application outside its intended use can reach".
candidates.threat_to_goal: None for the emulator. An application that passes a short value emits a wrong voucher committed in the outputs root, without any error.
candidates.evidence: Host build against the libcmt mock: echo '{"destination":"0x11..11","value":"0x01","payload":"0x"}' | rollup voucher -> index 0; the output bytes at value offset are 01 b5 4a ab 75 55 00 00 5b 00 ... (stack data).
candidates.test_idea: Run `rollup voucher` with value "0x01" (mock or in-machine) and assert it either exits non-zero or encodes value 1 (31 zero bytes then 01) in the emitted Voucher calldata.

candidates.title: Documented yield interface contradicts behavior: the manual says the next request type comes back in the DATA field, the yield tool's usage lists reasons it rejects, and the HTTP API says the first finish status is ignored
candidates.component: doc/README.md ('The /dev/cmio device' section) and machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 sys-utils/yield/yield.c, rollup-http-server /finish
candidates.role: Guest software (tools); the manual text is rated with what it documents
candidates.location: doc/README.md ~line 7236: "the host sets the `data` field on resume to HTIF_YIELD_REASON_ADVANCE_STATE or HTIF_YIELD_REASON_INSPECT_STATE". This contradicts ~line 7666 ("The REASON field in fromhost carries the request type, and the DATA field carries the request length"), src/send-cmio-response.cpp (reason<<32 | length) and libcmt unpack(). yield.c help() and the manual (~7264) list "tx-voucher", "tx-notice", while get_reason() accepts only "tx-output", "tx-report", ... . openapi rollup.yaml /finish: "The Rollup HTTP Server ignores the content of the status field for the first finish request and after an inspect-state request", while http_service.rs finish() always passes accept=false for "reject" to cmt_rollup_finish, which yields rx-rejected.
candidates.description: (a) A tool or binding written to the manual's /dev/cmio description reads the request type from fromhost DATA. That field holds the input length, at least 292 for any EvmAdvance, so every advance is misclassified. (b) A shell application emitting outputs with `yield automatic tx-notice <len>`, as the documented usage lists, gets 'Invalid <reason> argument', exit 1, and no yield. (c) An HTTP application that starts its loop with status 'reject', which the API says is ignored, makes the server issue an rx-rejected manual yield before any input. The machine then never reaches the accepted yield a valid template needs, so every delivery is a no-op. All three are deterministic contradictions between the documentation and the behavior in the yield interface. None is triggered by an input.
candidates.trigger: Application developer following the documentation. No input sender involvement.
candidates.reachability: Deterministic at development or template-build time. A developer would likely notice before deployment, since nothing works.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? Not excluded, but there is no input trigger.

2 Role: yield tool and rollup-http-server are Guest software; the /dev/cmio text is part of the manual. THREAT_MODEL.md section 3, Guest software: "A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low." Section 8: "A contradiction between the manual and the behavior on a security-relevant point is a defect in one of the two. It takes the severity it would have if the manual were right."

3 High/Medium: the Medium entry "An undocumented deterministic deviation, consistent across all paths, in behavior that no correct guest relies on" does not fit, since a guest that follows the text does rely on it. If the manual's (a) were right, the emulator would deviate in R7 "reason encoding". The manual itself is internally inconsistent, though, and its HTIF section matches the code.

4 Critical only if triage takes the /dev/cmio text as the normative one (then the emulator and libcmt deviate from the documented yield interface, R7). That is unlikely given the authoritative HTIF section.
5 Low: documentation and tool contradictions that a documented application hits deterministically, with no input involvement, so no rule is violated at a reachable state.
candidates.threat_to_goal: None directly. These are documentation defects in the yield interface, the area R7 names, that can lead application or binding authors to misread request types, fail to emit outputs, or build an invalid template.
candidates.evidence: Code and document reading. yield.c get_reason() table versus help(); send-cmio-response.cpp line 81; rollup.yaml /finish description versus http_service.rs finish().
candidates.test_idea: (b) In a machine, run `yield automatic tx-notice 0` and assert exit 0 with an automatic yield whose reason is TX_OUTPUT, or fix the usage text. (c) Start rollup-http-server with a client whose first POST /finish has status 'reject', and assert the machine reaches an rx-accepted yield. (a) Is a text fix, checked by grepping the manual for the DATA/REASON statement.

not_covered: rollup-http-server was not built or run (no Rust build attempted); its behavior is from code reading only, including actix panic or worker behavior on malformed requests (`&payload[2..]` slicing without a 0x check panics on short or non-ASCII strings) and concurrency between workers sharing RollupFd

Linux cmio kernel driver semantics (single-open, ioctl error paths after a completed yield, interaction with signals); the kernel is out of scope, but libcmt's yield-then-push ordering depends on them
GIO (cmt_gio_request, rollup gio, /gio) and inspect-state paths: in PRT they lead to a stall or are outside verified history; not analysed beyond a read
rollup-http-client crate, echo-dapp, hex tool, misc utilities (writemmap/readmmap/memoryrange), xhalt, labelinfo
libcmt big-endian code paths (keccakf has a dubious cast under __BYTE_ORDER__ != LITTLE) since the guest is little-endian RISC-V

cartesi-init and rollup-init end-to-end in a real machine (rollup-init's `rollup exception` with a non-hex payload fails, so no exception is registered when rollup-http-server dies; not tested, leads to a halt either way)
No in-machine end-to-end run with the guest-tools rootfs; all dynamic checks used the libcmt mock on the host

libcmt keccak and outputs-Merkle tree were checked differentially against cartesi.keccak256 for lengths 0..1100 and roots for 0..40 leaves (all equal); deeper leaf counts (state[i] for large i) were not exercised beyond the pristine-root check
On-chain output validation (LibOutputValidityProof) was only checked for height and leaf hashing consistency, not audited
